claim: In higher eukaryotes, the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) contains a network of membrane tubules.
source: In higher eukaryotes, the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) contains a network of membrane tubules, which transitions into sheets during mitosis.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about ER morphology in higher eukaryotes, supported by the manuscript's introduction and cited literature.

claim: The ER network transitions into sheets during mitosis.
source: In higher eukaryotes, the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) contains a network of membrane tubules, which transitions into sheets during mitosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to previous work and experimental data shown in the manuscript.

claim: Network formation involves curvature-stabilizing proteins, including the reticulons (Rtns).
source: Network formation involves curvature-stabilizing proteins, including the reticulons (Rtns), as well as the membrane-fusing GTPase atlastin (ATL) and the lunapark protein (Lnp).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature and experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Network formation involves the membrane-fusing GTPase atlastin (ATL).
source: Network formation involves curvature-stabilizing proteins, including the reticulons (Rtns), as well as the membrane-fusing GTPase atlastin (ATL) and the lunapark protein (Lnp).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature and experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Network formation involves the lunapark protein (Lnp).
source: Network formation involves curvature-stabilizing proteins, including the reticulons (Rtns), as well as the membrane-fusing GTPase atlastin (ATL) and the lunapark protein (Lnp).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature and experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: ATL is needed to form the ER network.
source: ATL is needed to not only form, but also maintain, the ER network.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with dominant-negative ATL mutants and cytATL fragments in both mammalian cells and Xenopus extracts.

claim: ATL is needed to maintain the ER network.
source: ATL is needed to not only form, but also maintain, the ER network.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments showing that inhibition of ATL in preformed networks causes disassembly.

claim: Maintenance of the ER network requires a balance between ATL and Rtn.
source: Maintenance requires a balance between ATL and Rtn, as too little ATL activity or too high Rtn4a concentrations cause ER fragmentation.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that overexpression of Rtn4a causes fragmentation that can be rescued by co-overexpression of ATL.

claim: Too little ATL activity causes ER fragmentation.
source: Maintenance requires a balance between ATL and Rtn, as too little ATL activity or too high Rtn4a concentrations cause ER fragmentation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with dominant-negative ATL mutants.

claim: Too high Rtn4a concentrations cause ER fragmentation.
source: Maintenance requires a balance between ATL and Rtn, as too little ATL activity or too high Rtn4a concentrations cause ER fragmentation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments showing fragmentation in cells overexpressing Rtn4a.

claim: Lnp only affects the abundance of three-way junctions and tubules.
source: Lnp only affects the abundance of three-way junctions and tubules.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with Lnp knockout cells and cytLnp inhibition in Xenopus extracts.

claim: ATL-mediated fusion counteracts the instability of free tubule ends.
source: We suggest a model in which ATL-mediated fusion counteracts the instability of free tubule ends.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental observations and reasoning presented in the manuscript.

claim: ATL tethers and fuses tubules stabilized by the Rtns.
source: ATL tethers and fuses tubules stabilized by the Rtns, and transiently sits in newly formed three-way junctions.
evidence: This is supported by localization studies and functional experiments.

claim: ATL transiently sits in newly formed three-way junctions.
source: ATL tethers and fuses tubules stabilized by the Rtns, and transiently sits in newly formed three-way junctions.
evidence: This is supported by localization studies showing ATL at three-way junctions.

claim: Lnp subsequently moves into the junctional sheets.
source: Lnp subsequently moves into the junctional sheets and forms oligomers.
evidence: This is inferred from localization studies and the temporal relationship between ATL and Lnp function.

claim: Lnp forms oligomers.
source: Lnp subsequently moves into the junctional sheets and forms oligomers.
evidence: This is supported by pull-down experiments and gel filtration analysis.

claim: Lnp is inactivated by mitotic phosphorylation.
source: Lnp is inactivated by mitotic phosphorylation, which contributes to the tubule-to-sheet conversion of the ER.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data showing mitotic phosphorylation and experiments with phosphomimetic mutants.

claim: Mitotic phosphorylation of Lnp contributes to the tubule-to-sheet conversion of the ER.
source: Lnp is inactivated by mitotic phosphorylation, which contributes to the tubule-to-sheet conversion of the ER.
evidence: This is supported by the observation that Lnp inactivation mimics mitotic ER morphology and that Lnp is phosphorylated during mitosis.

claim: In interphase, the ER consists of the nuclear envelope and a connected peripheral network of tubules and interspersed sheets.
source: In interphase, the ER consists of the nuclear envelope and a connected peripheral network of tubules and interspersed sheets (Shibata et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2013; English and Voeltz, 2013a; Goyal and Blackstone, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: The ER network is dynamic, with tubules continuously forming, retracting, and sliding along one another.
source: The network is dynamic, with tubules continuously forming, retracting, and sliding along one another.
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging observations.

claim: During mitosis in metazoans, the nuclear envelope disassembles and peripheral ER tubules are transformed into sheets.
source: During mitosis in metazoans, the nuclear envelope disassembles and peripheral ER tubules are transformed into sheets (Lu et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: The tubules themselves are shaped by two evolutionarily conserved protein families, the reticulons (Rtns) and DP1/Yop1p.
source: Previous work has suggested that the tubules themselves are shaped by two evolutionarily conserved protein families, the reticulons (Rtns) and DP1/Yop1p (Voeltz et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Rtns and DP1/Yop1p are abundant membrane proteins that are both necessary and sufficient to generate tubules.
source: These are abundant membrane proteins that are both necessary and sufficient to generate tubules.
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Members of the Rtns and DP1/Yop1p families are found in all eukaryotic cells.
source: Members of these families are found in all eukaryotic cells.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of protein family distribution.

claim: The Rtns and DP1/Yop1p seem to stabilize the high membrane curvature seen in cross-sections of tubules and sheet edges.
source: The Rtns and DP1/Yop1p seem to stabilize the high membrane curvature seen in cross-sections of tubules and sheet edges (Hu et al., 2008; Shibata et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Rtns and DP1/Yop1p all contain pairs of closely spaced trans-membrane segments.
source: How these proteins generate and stabilize membrane curvature is uncertain, but they all contain pairs of closely spaced trans-membrane segments and have an amphipathic helix that is required to generate tubules with reconstituted proteoliposomes (Brady et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Rtns and DP1/Yop1p have an amphipathic helix that is required to generate tubules with reconstituted proteoliposomes.
source: How these proteins generate and stabilize membrane curvature is uncertain, but they all contain pairs of closely spaced trans-membrane segments and have an amphipathic helix that is required to generate tubules with reconstituted proteoliposomes (Brady et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: It has been proposed that the Rtns and DP1/Yop1p form wedges in the lipid bilayer and arc-shaped oligomers around the tubules.
source: It has been proposed that the Rtns and DP1/Yop1p form wedges in the lipid bilayer and arc-shaped oligomers around the tubules (Hu et al., 2008; Shibata et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a model proposed in cited literature.

claim: Connecting tubules into a network requires membrane fusion, which is mediated by membrane-anchored GTPases, the atlastins (ATLs) in metazoans and Sey1p and related proteins in yeast and plants.
source: Connecting tubules into a network requires membrane fusion, which is mediated by membrane-anchored GTPases, the atlastins (ATLs) in metazoans and Sey1p and related proteins in yeast and plants (Hu et al., 2009; Orso et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: ATL proteins contain a cytoplasmic GTPase domain, followed by a helical bundle, two closely spaced trans-membrane segments, and a cytoplasmic tail.
source: These proteins contain a cytoplasmic GTPase domain, followed by a helical bundle, two closely spaced trans-membrane segments, and a cytoplasmic tail (Bian et al., 2011; Byrnes and Sondermann, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature describing ATL structure.

claim: Mammals have three isoforms of ATL, with ATL-1 being prominently expressed in neuronal cells.
source: Mammals have three isoforms of ATL, with ATL-1 being prominently expressed in neuronal cells.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of ATL isoforms.

claim: Mutations in ATL-1 can cause hereditary spastic paraplegia, a neurodegenerative disease that is characterized by the shortening of the axons in corticospinal motor neurons.
source: Mutations in ATL-1 can cause hereditary spastic paraplegia, a neurodegenerative disease that is characterized by the shortening of the axons in corticospinal motor neurons (Salinas et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Hereditary spastic paraplegia leads to progressive spasticity and weakness of the lower limbs.
source: This leads to progressive spasticity and weakness of the lower limbs.
evidence: This is a clinical description of the disease mentioned in the context of ATL-1 mutations.

claim: Proteoliposomes containing purified Drosophila ATL undergo GTP-dependent fusion in vitro.
source: A role for ATL in membrane fusion is supported by the fact that proteoliposomes containing purified Drosophila ATL undergo GTP-dependent fusion in vitro (Bian et al., 2011; Orso et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: The fusion of ER vesicles in Xenopus laevis egg extracts is prevented by the addition of ATL antibodies or a cytosolic fragment of ATL.
source: Furthermore, the fusion of ER vesicles in Xenopus laevis egg extracts is prevented by the addition of ATL antibodies or a cytosolic fragment of ATL (Hu et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: ATL-depleted Drosophila larvae have fragmented ER.
source: Finally, ATL-depleted Drosophila larvae have fragmented ER, and the depletion of ATL or expression of dominant-negative ATL mutants in tissue culture cells leads to long, unbranched tubules (Hu et al., 2009; Orso et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: The depletion of ATL or expression of dominant-negative ATL mutants in tissue culture cells leads to long, unbranched tubules.
source: Finally, ATL-depleted Drosophila larvae have fragmented ER, and the depletion of ATL or expression of dominant-negative ATL mutants in tissue culture cells leads to long, unbranched tubules (Hu et al., 2009; Orso et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature and confirmed by experiments in this manuscript.

claim: ATL molecules sitting in different membranes dimerize through their GTPase domains (trans-interaction).
source: Crystal structures and biochemical experiments have led to a model in which ATL molecules sitting in different membranes dimerize through their GTPase domains (trans-interaction), and undergo a conformational change during the GTPase cycle, thereby pulling the two membranes together and fusing them.
evidence: This is a model based on structural and biochemical studies cited in the literature.

claim: ATL molecules undergo a conformational change during the GTPase cycle, thereby pulling the two membranes together and fusing them.
source: Crystal structures and biochemical experiments have led to a model in which ATL molecules sitting in different membranes dimerize through their GTPase domains (trans-interaction), and undergo a conformational change during the GTPase cycle, thereby pulling the two membranes together and fusing them.
evidence: This is a model based on structural and biochemical studies cited in the literature.

claim: ATL molecules sitting in the same membrane can also form GTPase-dependent dimers (cis-interaction).
source: Interestingly, ATL molecules sitting in the same membrane can also form GTPase-dependent dimers (cis-interaction) (Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: The fusion of membrane tubules generates three-way junctions, which are small, triangular sheets with negatively curved edge lines.
source: The fusion of membrane tubules generates three-way junctions, which are small, triangular sheets with negatively curved edge lines (Shemesh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: It has been suggested that three-way junctions are stabilized by the lunapark protein (Lnp), a conserved membrane protein.
source: How junctions are maintained is unknown, but it has been suggested that they are stabilized by the lunapark protein (Lnp), a conserved membrane protein (Chen et al., 2012; Shemesh et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from cited literature.

claim: Lnp contains two closely spaced transmembrane segments and a Zn2+-finger domain.
source: Lnp contains two closely spaced transmembrane segments and a Zn2+-finger domain (Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Lnp localizes preferentially to three-way junctions.
source: Lnp localizes preferentially to three-way junctions, but there is disagreement as to whether it stabilizes newly formed three-way junctions (in mammalian cells), or functions in ring closure, i.e. the disappearance of junctions (in yeast) (Chen et al., 2012; Shemesh et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature and confirmed by experiments in this manuscript.

claim: Sey1p and some isoforms of ATL also localize to three-way junctions.
source: Furthermore, Sey1p and some isoforms of ATL also localize to three-way junctions and could therefore play a role in their stabilization (Hu et al., 2009; English and Voeltz, 2013b; Yan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Live-cell imaging by spinning-disk confocal microscopy of U2OS cells expressing GFP-calreticulin revealed both a tubular network and interdispersed sheet-like structures.
source: Live-cell imaging by spinning-disk confocal microscopy revealed both a tubular network and interdispersed sheet-like structures (Figure 1A; first column; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The expression of wild type ATL isoforms had only a moderate effect on ER morphology.
source: The expression of wild type ATL isoforms had only a moderate effect on ER morphology (Figure 1A; second and third columns; Figure 1—figure supplement1B,C).
evidence: This is observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Fluorescently tagged wild type ATL-1 localized throughout tubules.
source: Fluorescently tagged wild type ATL-1 localized throughout tubules (Figure 1A; second column), whereas wild type ATL-3 and ATL-2 localized in punctae at three-way junctions (Figure 1A; third column; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, respectively).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Wild type ATL-3 and ATL-2 localized in punctae at three-way junctions.
source: Fluorescently tagged wild type ATL-1 localized throughout tubules (Figure 1A; second column), whereas wild type ATL-3 and ATL-2 localized in punctae at three-way junctions (Figure 1A; third column; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, respectively).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Dimerization-defective ATL-1 or ATL-3 mutants, carrying the R217Q or R213Q mutations, distributed throughout the ER.
source: Dimerization-defective ATL-1 or ATL-3 mutants, carrying the R217Q or R213Q mutations (Byrnes and Sondermann, 2011), respectively, distributed throughout the ER (Figure 1A, fourth and fifth column).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The punctate localization of ATL-3 to three-way junctions is due to its dimerization with endogenous ATL.
source: Thus, the punctate localization of ATL-3 to three-way junctions is due to its dimerization with endogenous ATL.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that dimerization-defective mutants do not localize to junctions.

claim: The different localization patterns of ATL-1 and ATL-3 have been attributed to the fact that ATL-1 hydrolyzes GTP faster than ATL-3.
source: The different localization patterns of ATL-1 and ATL-3 have been attributed to the fact that ATL-1 hydrolyzes GTP faster than ATL-3; faster GTP hydrolysis would lead to less concentration in junctions (Yan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an explanation from cited literature.

claim: Expression of ATL-1 K80A caused the conversion of most of the ER into small vesicles, which rapidly moved around the cell.
source: Expression of ATL-1 K80A caused the conversion of most of the ER into small vesicles, which rapidly moved around the cell, as shown by time-lapse imaging (Figure 1B; first column; the lowest row shows three different time points with different colors; see also Video 1).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images and videos.

claim: In many cells expressing ATL-1 K80A, long, unbranched tubules were also seen.
source: In many cells, long, unbranched tubules were also seen (Figure 1B; second column; Video 2).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images and videos.

claim: The long membrane tubules in cells expressing ATL-1 K80A were aligned with microtubules and seemed to be pulled out from a membrane reservoir near the nucleus after cell division.
source: These membrane tubules were aligned with microtubules and seemed to be pulled out from a membrane reservoir near the nucleus after cell division (not shown).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claim: Treatment of cells expressing ATL-1 K80A with the microtubule-disassembling drug nocodazole led to the disappearance of the long membrane tubules.
source: Indeed, treatment of the cells with the microtubule-disassembling drug nocodazole led to the disappearance of the long membrane tubules (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Expression of a double mutant of ATL-1, which is both GTPase- and dimerization- defective (ATL-1 K80A R217Q) left the reticular ER intact.
source: Expression of a double mutant of ATL-1, which is both GTPase- and dimerization- defective (ATL-1 K80A R217Q) left the reticular ER intact (Figure 1B; third column), demonstrating that the ATL-1 K80A mutant causes ER morphology changes by forming inactive dimers with endogenous ATL.
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The ATL-1 K80A mutant causes ER morphology changes by forming inactive dimers with endogenous ATL.
source: Expression of a double mutant of ATL-1, which is both GTPase- and dimerization- defective (ATL-1 K80A R217Q) left the reticular ER intact (Figure 1B; third column), demonstrating that the ATL-1 K80A mutant causes ER morphology changes by forming inactive dimers with endogenous ATL.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the double mutant does not affect ER morphology.

claim: Vesiculation of the ER was also observed with dominant-negative, GTPase-defective ATL-2 or ATL-3 mutants.
source: Vesiculation of the ER was also observed with dominant-negative, GTPase-defective ATL-2 or ATL-3 mutants (ATL-3 K73A or ATL-2 K107A; Figure 1B; fourth column; Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, respectively).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images.

claim: Expression of a cytoplasmic fragment of the GTPase-defective, dominant-negative ATL-1 K80A mutant (cytATL-1-K80A-mCherry) converted the ER into long, unbranched tubules at low expression levels.
source: Expression of a cytoplasmic fragment of the GTPase-defective, dominant-negative ATL-1 K80A mutant (cytATL-1-K80A-mCherry) converted the ER into long, unbranched tubules at low expression levels (Figure 1C; second column), and into small vesicles at high levels (third column).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Expression of a cytoplasmic fragment of the GTPase-defective, dominant-negative ATL-1 K80A mutant (cytATL-1-K80A-mCherry) converted the ER into small vesicles at high expression levels.
source: Expression of a cytoplasmic fragment of the GTPase-defective, dominant-negative ATL-1 K80A mutant (cytATL-1-K80A-mCherry) converted the ER into long, unbranched tubules at low expression levels (Figure 1C; second column), and into small vesicles at high levels (third column).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A cytoplasmic fragment of wild type ATL-1 (cytATL-1-mCherry) only generated long, unbranched tubules, even at high expression levels.
source: A cytoplasmic fragment of wild type ATL-1 (cytATL-1-mCherry) only generated long, unbranched tubules, even at high expression levels (fourth column), likely because it interacts with endogenous ATL only transiently during the GTPase cycle and is therefore a weaker inhibitor than cytATL-1 K80A.
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 1C.

claim: CytATL-1 K80A localized more prominently to the ER than wild type cytATL-1.
source: Consistent with this assumption, cytATL-1 K80A localized more prominently to the ER than wild type cytATL-1 (not shown), and non-dimerizing versions of cytATL-1 K80A or cytATL-1, which carry the R217Q mutation (Byrnes and Sondermann, 2011), did not affect the morphology of the ER (columns five and six).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claim: Non-dimerizing versions of cytATL-1 K80A or cytATL-1, which carry the R217Q mutation, did not affect the morphology of the ER.
source: Consistent with this assumption, cytATL-1 K80A localized more prominently to the ER than wild type cytATL-1 (not shown), and non-dimerizing versions of cytATL-1 K80A or cytATL-1, which carry the R217Q mutation (Byrnes and Sondermann, 2011), did not affect the morphology of the ER (columns five and six).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 1C.

claim: An ER network can be generated from membrane fragments in a crude interphase Xenopus egg extract.
source: As reported previously, an ER network can be generated from membrane fragment in a crude interphase extract (Figure 2A); network formation is prevented when membrane fusion is inhibited by the addition of a dominant-negative cytoplasmic fragment of Xenopus ATL (cytATL) at the beginning of the reaction (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 2A and supported by cited literature.

claim: Network formation in Xenopus extracts is prevented when membrane fusion is inhibited by the addition of a dominant-negative cytoplasmic fragment of Xenopus ATL (cytATL) at the beginning of the reaction.
source: As reported previously, an ER network can be generated from membrane fragment in a crude interphase extract (Figure 2A); network formation is prevented when membrane fusion is inhibited by the addition of a dominant-negative cytoplasmic fragment of Xenopus ATL (cytATL) at the beginning of the reaction (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: CytATL disassembled a preformed ER network in Xenopus extracts.
source: Surprisingly, we found that cytATL also disassembled a preformed network. At low concentrations, a fragmented tubular network remained (Figure 2B). At higher concentrations, only small membrane structures were observed (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: At low concentrations of cytATL, a fragmented tubular network remained.
source: Surprisingly, we found that cytATL also disassembled a preformed network. At low concentrations, a fragmented tubular network remained (Figure 2B). At higher concentrations, only small membrane structures were observed (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 2B.

claim: At higher concentrations of cytATL, only small membrane structures were observed.
source: Surprisingly, we found that cytATL also disassembled a preformed network. At low concentrations, a fragmented tubular network remained (Figure 2B). At higher concentrations, only small membrane structures were observed (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A non-dimerizing mutant of cytATL (cytATL R232Q) had no effect on the integrity of the network.
source: A non-dimerizing mutant of cytATL (cytATL R232Q) had no effect on the integrity of the network (Figure 2D), likely because it did not bind to the endogenous ATL.
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Inhibition of endogenous ATL by addition of GTPγS also disassembled the network.
source: Inhibition of endogenous ATL by addition of GTPγS also disassembled the network (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Similar results were obtained with a fractionated system, consisting either of Xenopus membranes and membrane-depleted cytosol or of membranes only.
source: Similar results were obtained with a fractionated system, consisting either of Xenopus membranes and membrane-depleted cytosol (Figure 2F) or of membranes only (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ATL function is not only required to form an ER network, but also to maintain it.
source: These results indicate that ATL function is not only required to form an ER network, but also to maintain it.
evidence: This is concluded from the experiments showing network disassembly upon ATL inhibition.

claim: ATL was also required to maintain an ER network in mitotic (meiotic) Xenopus extracts.
source: ATL was also required to maintain an ER network in mitotic (meiotic) extracts. A dimerization-defective cytATL-R232Q mutant did not affect the mitotic ER network; as in untreated mitotic extracts (Wang et al., 2013), many small sheets connected by short tubules were seen (Figure 2G). In contrast, blocking the function of endogenous ATL by addition of cytATL resulted in the disassembly of the network (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 2G and 2H.

claim: A dimerization-defective cytATL-R232Q mutant did not affect the mitotic ER network.
source: ATL was also required to maintain an ER network in mitotic (meiotic) extracts. A dimerization-defective cytATL-R232Q mutant did not affect the mitotic ER network; as in untreated mitotic extracts (Wang et al., 2013), many small sheets connected by short tubules were seen (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Blocking the function of endogenous ATL by addition of cytATL resulted in the disassembly of the mitotic ER network.
source: In contrast, blocking the function of endogenous ATL by addition of cytATL resulted in the disassembly of the network (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 2H.

claim: When cytATL-GFP arrived in the chamber, the network disassembled, starting at the site where cytATL-GFP arrived.
source: When cytATL-GFP arrived in the chamber, the network disassembled, starting at the site where cytATL-GFP arrived (Figure 3; Video 3).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images and video shown in Figure 3 and Video 3.

claim: Close observation of the disassembly reaction showed that tubules frequently first detach from one another before they crumble and convert into smaller structures.
source: Close observation of the disassembly reaction showed that tubules frequently first detach from one another (arrows) before they crumble and convert into smaller structures (Figure 3).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 3.

claim: The initial detachment of the tubules suggests that some three-way junctions contained tethered, rather than fused tubules, and that ATL inactivation caused their untethering.
source: The initial detachment of the tubules suggests that some three-way junctions contained tethered, rather than fused tubules, and that ATL inactivation caused their untethering.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of tubule detachment during network disassembly.

claim: The final structures of network disassembly were larger than the small vesicles that serve as starting material for network formation.
source: The final structures of network disassembly were larger than the small vesicles that serve as starting material for network formation.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claim: Dynamic sheets were seen from which short tubules emerge and retract during early time points of network formation.
source: Occasionally, dynamic sheets were seen from which short tubules emerge and retract (not shown). These structures are possibly explained by residual ATL activity. They were much more abundant during early time points of network formation (Figure 4A), or if network formation was slowed down by partial inhibition of ATL, for example, by adding a low concentration of GTP to a membrane-only reaction (Figure 4B), or by adding GDP and AlF4- to a reaction consisting of membranes and cytosol (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 4A, 4B, and 4C.

claim: During network formation, ATL first mediates the fusion of small vesicles into small, dynamic structures, which subsequently give rise to longer tubules.
source: These results indicate that during network formation, ATL first mediates the fusion of small vesicles into small, dynamic structures, which subsequently give rise to longer tubules.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of intermediates during network formation.

claim: Inactivation of ATL disassembles the tubules into small membrane structures.
source: Inactivation of ATL disassembles the tubules into small membrane structures.
evidence: This is directly observed in the experiments with cytATL and GTPγS.

claim: At endogenous levels, the reticulons and DP1 are insufficient to maintain the integrity of tubules in the absence of ATL function.
source: Our experiments also indicate that, at endogenous levels, the reticulons and DP1 are insufficient to maintain the integrity of tubules in the absence of ATL function.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that tubules disassemble when ATL is inactivated.

claim: Functional ATL localized mostly to three-way junctions in an ER network assembled from crude Xenopus extracts.
source: Functional ATL localized mostly to three-way junctions in an ER network assembled from crude Xenopus extracts, as demonstrated by the addition of fluorescently labeled, affinity-purified antibodies raised against Xenopus ATL (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 5A.

claim: When cytATL labeled with the fluorescent dye Alexa 488 was added at low concentrations, the label was seen throughout the tubules.
source: In contrast, when cytATL labeled with the fluorescent dye Alexa 488 was added at low concentrations, the label was seen throughout the tubules (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 5B.

claim: CytATL molecules likely represent inactive dimers formed with endogenous ATL.
source: These molecules likely represent inactive dimers formed with endogenous ATL; the fraction of inactivated endogenous ATL is apparently small enough to maintain the integrity of the network.
evidence: This is inferred from the localization pattern and the fact that the network remains intact.

claim: Antibodies to Xenopus ATL stained three-way junctions in a fractionated system consisting of membranes and cytosol.
source: Similar results were obtained with a fractionated system, consisting of membranes and cytosol. Again, antibodies to Xenopus ATL stained three-way junctions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), whereas cytATL-GFP stained the entire network (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B; left panel).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CytATL-GFP stained the entire network in a fractionated system consisting of membranes and cytosol.
source: Similar results were obtained with a fractionated system, consisting of membranes and cytosol. Again, antibodies to Xenopus ATL stained three-way junctions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), whereas cytATL-GFP stained the entire network (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B; left panel).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CytATL R232Q-GFP, which fails to bind endogenous ATL, localized to the cytosol.
source: As expected, cytATL R232Q-GFP, which fails to bind endogenous ATL, localized to the cytosol (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B; rightmost panel).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Functional ATL localizes to three-way junctions, whereas inactivated ATL distributes throughout the tubules.
source: These results indicate that functional ATL localizes to three-way junctions, whereas inactivated ATL distributes throughout the tubules.
evidence: This is concluded from the localization patterns of antibodies to ATL and cytATL.

claim: Inhibition of ATL function affected network formation more than network maintenance.
source: We noticed that inhibition of ATL function affected network formation more than network maintenance.
evidence: This is observed in experiments with GDP-BeF3- and GTPγS.

claim: The addition of low concentrations of GDP plus BeF3- prevented the de novo formation of an ER network, but left a pre-formed network intact.
source: The addition of low concentrations of GDP plus BeF3-, a mixture that locks endogenous ATL into an inactive, dimeric state, prevented the de novo formation of an ER network, but left a pre-formed network intact (Figure 6).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 6.

claim: At higher concentrations of GDP plus BeF3-, both network formation and maintenance were affected.
source: At higher concentrations, both network formation and maintenance were affected.
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 6.

claim: The de novo formation of an ER network is more sensitive to ATL inhibition than the maintenance of a preformed network.
source: These experiments show that the de novo formation of an ER network is more sensitive to ATL inhibition than the maintenance of a preformed network.
evidence: This is concluded from the differential effects of low and high concentrations of ATL inhibitors.

claim: At low expression levels, mCherry-Rtn4a distributed together with GFP-calreticulin throughout the tubules of the ER.
source: At low expression levels, mCherry-Rtn4a distributed together with GFP-calreticulin throughout the tubules of the ER (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 7A.

claim: At higher levels of Rtn4a expression, unbranched tubules were seen.
source: At higher levels, unbranched tubules were seen (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Unbranched tubules formed by high Rtn4a expression were often depleted of GFP-calreticulin, suggesting that these were too narrow to accommodate luminal proteins.
source: Often these tubules were depleted of GFP-calreticulin, suggesting that these were too narrow to accommodate luminal proteins, as observed previously in transient overexpression experiments (Hu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 7B and supported by cited literature.

claim: In addition to unbranched tubules, some of the ER was fragmented in cells overexpressing Rtn4a.
source: In addition, some of the ER was fragmented; the membrane fragments contained both GFP-calreticulin and mCherry-Rtn4 and moved rapidly (Figure 7C; Video 6), but they seemed to be larger than in cells expressing dominant-negative ATL mutants (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images and videos shown in Figure 7C and Video 6.

claim: The membrane fragments in cells overexpressing Rtn4a contained both GFP-calreticulin and mCherry-Rtn4 and moved rapidly.
source: In addition, some of the ER was fragmented; the membrane fragments contained both GFP-calreticulin and mCherry-Rtn4 and moved rapidly (Figure 7C; Video 6), but they seemed to be larger than in cells expressing dominant-negative ATL mutants (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images and videos shown in Figure 7C and Video 6.

claim: The membrane fragments in cells overexpressing Rtn4a seemed to be larger than in cells expressing dominant-negative ATL mutants.
source: In addition, some of the ER was fragmented; the membrane fragments contained both GFP-calreticulin and mCherry-Rtn4 and moved rapidly (Figure 7C; Video 6), but they seemed to be larger than in cells expressing dominant-negative ATL mutants (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a comparative observation from the microscopy images.

claim: Fragmentation of the ER by overexpression of Rtn4a had not been observed in fixed cells.
source: Fragmentation of the ER by overexpression of Rtn4a had not been observed in fixed cells, again highlighting the need for live-cell imaging.
evidence: This is a statement about previous observations and the advantages of live-cell imaging.

claim: The co-overexpression of Rtn4a and wild type ATL-1 or ATL-3 restored the integrity of the network, making the membrane fragments disappear and returning tubular junctions.
source: The co-overexpression of Rtn4a and wild type ATL-1 or ATL-3 restored the integrity of the network, making the membrane fragments disappear and returning tubular junctions (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 7D.

claim: This effect is due to the fusion activity of ATL because the co-expression of the dimerization-defective ATL-1 R217Q mutant did not restore the network.
source: This effect is due to the fusion activity of ATL because the co-expression of the dimerization-defective ATL-1 R217Q mutant did not restore the network (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The co-overexpression of the dominant-negative ATL1- K80A mutant and Rtn4a resulted in both long, unbranched tubules and small vesicles.
source: As expected, the co-overexpression of the dominant-negative ATL1- K80A mutant and Rtn4a resulted in both long, unbranched tubules and small vesicles (Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Rtn4a and ATL seemed to segregate at least partially in cells co-overexpressing both proteins.
source: Interestingly, Rtn4a and ATL seemed to segregate at least partially, perhaps because Rtn displaces ATL molecules from long tubules.
evidence: This is observed in the microscopy images.

claim: An appropriate balance between ATL and Rtn4a is required for network formation.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that an appropriate balance between ATL and Rtn4a is required for network formation; too little ATL function, or too much Rtn4a, results in similar morphology defects, i.e. long, unbranched tubules and fragmented ER.
evidence: This is concluded from the experiments with Rtn4a overexpression and ATL inhibition.

claim: Too little ATL function, or too much Rtn4a, results in similar morphology defects, i.e. long, unbranched tubules and fragmented ER.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that an appropriate balance between ATL and Rtn4a is required for network formation; too little ATL function, or too much Rtn4a, results in similar morphology defects, i.e. long, unbranched tubules and fragmented ER.
evidence: This is concluded from the experiments with Rtn4a overexpression and ATL inhibition.

claim: Cells lacking Lnp exhibited a proliferation of peripheral sheets and a reduction of tubules and junctions.
source: Cells lacking Lnp exhibited a proliferation of peripheral sheets and a reduction of tubules and junctions (Figure 8A; quantification in Figure 8B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 8A and quantified in Figure 8B.

claim: The tubular network did not completely disappear in all cells lacking Lnp.
source: However, the tubular network did not completely disappear in all cells.
evidence: This is observed in the microscopy images of Lnp knockout cells.

claim: Immunostaining with reticulon antibodies showed that the residual tubular ER was often pushed to the periphery of the cells lacking Lnp.
source: Immunostaining with reticulon antibodies showed that the residual tubular ER was often pushed to the periphery of the cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Lnp is not essential to form tubules or three-way junctions, but it affects their abundance.
source: Thus, Lnp is not essential to form tubules or three-way junctions, but it affects their abundance.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that some tubules and junctions remain in Lnp knockout cells.

claim: These results are consistent with the ER morphology reported for a Lnp knock-out in S. cerevisiae.
source: These results are consistent with the ER morphology reported for a Lnp knock-out in S. cerevisiae (Chen et al., 2012), although the small cell size of this organism makes the distinction between tubules and sheets difficult.
evidence: This is a comparison with cited literature.

claim: When a fusion of wild type Lnp with mCherry (Lnp-mCherry) was stably expressed at low levels in CRISPR knock-out cells, the reticular network was restored.
source: When a fusion of wild type Lnp with mCherry (Lnp-mCherry) was stably expressed at low levels in CRISPR knock-out cells, the reticular network was restored; peripheral sheets were reduced in favor of tubules and junctions (Figure 8C; second column).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Lnp-mCherry localized preferentially to punctae at three-way junctions.
source: Lnp-mCherry localized preferentially to punctae at three-way junctions (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 8C.

claim: At higher expression levels of Lnp-mCherry, Lnp-containing sheets became more prominent.
source: At higher expression levels, Lnp-containing sheets became more prominent (Figure 8D), and at still higher levels, tubular structures with extremely large diameters were formed (>500 nm; Figure 8D; Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 8D.

claim: At still higher levels of Lnp-mCherry expression, tubular structures with extremely large diameters were formed (>500 nm).
source: At higher expression levels, Lnp-containing sheets became more prominent (Figure 8D), and at still higher levels, tubular structures with extremely large diameters were formed (>500 nm; Figure 8D; Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 8D and Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A Lnp mutant, in which the N-terminal myristoylation site was abolished (G2A mutation), failed to localize to junctions.
source: A Lnp mutant, in which the N-terminal myristoylation site was abolished (G2A mutation), failed to localize to junctions (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 9B.

claim: When a short, unrelated linker sequence was inserted after CC1 or before CC2, Lnp no longer concentrated in punctae.
source: Likewise, when a short, unrelated linker sequence was inserted after CC1 (Figure 9B) or before CC2 (not shown), Lnp no longer concentrated in punctae (Figure 9B), suggesting that the two coiled-coil domains need to be in register.
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The two coiled-coil domains of Lnp need to be in register for proper localization.
source: Likewise, when a short, unrelated linker sequence was inserted after CC1 (Figure 9B) or before CC2 (not shown), Lnp no longer concentrated in punctae (Figure 9B), suggesting that the two coiled-coil domains need to be in register.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that linker insertions disrupt localization.

claim: Truncation of Lnp before the Zn2+-finger domain abolished Lnp localization to three-way junctions.
source: Finally, truncation of Lnp before the Zn2+-finger domain also abolished Lnp localization to three-way junctions, whereas a truncation at a more C-terminal site had no effect (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 9B.

claim: A truncation of Lnp at a more C-terminal site had no effect on localization to three-way junctions.
source: Finally, truncation of Lnp before the Zn2+-finger domain also abolished Lnp localization to three-way junctions, whereas a truncation at a more C-terminal site had no effect (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Localization of Lnp to three-way junctions correlated with the conversion of peripheral sheets into a tubular network.
source: In all cases, localization of Lnp to three-way junctions correlated with the conversion of peripheral sheets into a tubular network, indicating that Lnp exerts its effect on ER morphology at junctions.
evidence: This is observed across all the Lnp mutant experiments.

claim: Lnp exerts its effect on ER morphology at junctions.
source: In all cases, localization of Lnp to three-way junctions correlated with the conversion of peripheral sheets into a tubular network, indicating that Lnp exerts its effect on ER morphology at junctions.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between localization and morphology changes.

claim: At high levels, all Lnp mutants generated sheets and aberrant structures.
source: At high levels, all Lnp mutants generated sheets and aberrant structures (not shown).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claim: Localization to three-way junctions requires several Lnp features, including the Zn2+-finger implicated in dimerization.
source: Taken together, these results show that localization to three-way junctions requires several Lnp features, including the Zn2+-finger implicated in dimerization.
evidence: This is concluded from the mutant analysis.

claim: Pull-down experiments with extracts of mammalian cells expressing different Lnp constructs show that the region containing the Zn2+-finger is required for Lnp-Lnp interaction.
source: Indeed, pull-down experiments with extracts of mammalian cells expressing different Lnp constructs show that the region containing the Zn2+-finger is required for Lnp-Lnp interaction (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the pull-down experiments shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The large sheets observed when Lnp-mCherry was expressed at high level in wild type U2OS cells disappeared when wild type GFP-ATL-3 or GFP-ATL-1 were co-expressed.
source: The large sheets observed when Lnp-mCherry was expressed at high level in wild type U2OS cells disappeared when wild type GFP-ATL-3 or GFP-ATL-1 were co-expressed (Figure 10A; compare second and third with first column).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 10A.

claim: The ER network was restored when wild type GFP-ATL-3 or GFP-ATL-1 were co-expressed with Lnp-mCherry.
source: The ER network was restored, and the ATL proteins localized as in wild type cells.
evidence: This is observed in the microscopy images.

claim: GFP-ATL-3 was always close to Lnp-mCherry, and was often found at the edges of the Lnp-containing structures, but the two proteins did not co-localize.
source: GFP-ATL-3 was always close to Lnp-mCherry, and was often found at the edges of the Lnp-containing structures, but the two proteins did not co-localize (Figure 10A; second column).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 10A.

claim: Expression of GFP-ATL-1 caused Lnp-mCherry to redistribute from large to small sheet-like structures.
source: Expression of GFP-ATL-1 also caused Lnp-mCherry to redistribute from large to small sheet-like structures (Figure 10A; third column), even though ATL-1 itself localized mostly throughout the tubules.
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 10A.

claim: ATL affects the localization of Lnp, although the bulk of ATL and Lnp do not seem to interact physically.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that ATL affects the localization of Lnp, although the bulk of ATL and Lnp do not seem to interact physically.
evidence: This is concluded from the localization studies and pull-down experiments.

claim: No interaction between ATL and Lnp was seen in pull-down experiments.
source: In agreement with this conclusion, no interaction was seen in pull-down experiments (not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments.

claim: ATL functions upstream of Lnp.
source: Our experiments also suggest that ATL functions upstream of Lnp, a conclusion that is supported by the observation that Lnp overexpression did not significantly affect the localization of the ATLs (Figure 10A), and did not reverse ER fragmentation in cells expressing dominant-negative ATL mutants (Figure 10—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Lnp overexpression does not affect ATL localization or rescue ATL mutant phenotypes.

claim: Lnp overexpression did not significantly affect the localization of the ATLs.
source: Our experiments also suggest that ATL functions upstream of Lnp, a conclusion that is supported by the observation that Lnp overexpression did not significantly affect the localization of the ATLs (Figure 10A), and did not reverse ER fragmentation in cells expressing dominant-negative ATL mutants (Figure 10—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 10A.

claim: Lnp overexpression did not reverse ER fragmentation in cells expressing dominant-negative ATL mutants.
source: Our experiments also suggest that ATL functions upstream of Lnp, a conclusion that is supported by the observation that Lnp overexpression did not significantly affect the localization of the ATLs (Figure 10A), and did not reverse ER fragmentation in cells expressing dominant-negative ATL mutants (Figure 10—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The stable expression of wild type ATL in Lnp-lacking cells converted peripheral ER sheets into tubules and junctions.
source: The stable expression of wild type ATL in Lnp-lacking cells converted peripheral ER sheets into tubules and junctions (Figure 10B; second and third column), whereas dominant-negative ATL mutants fragmented the ER or led to long, unbranched tubules (Figure 10—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 10B.

claim: Dominant-negative ATL mutants fragmented the ER or led to long, unbranched tubules in Lnp-lacking cells.
source: The stable expression of wild type ATL in Lnp-lacking cells converted peripheral ER sheets into tubules and junctions (Figure 10B; second and third column), whereas dominant-negative ATL mutants fragmented the ER or led to long, unbranched tubules (Figure 10—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Low-level expression of Rtn4a in Lnp knock-out cells resulted in restoration of the tubular network.
source: Similarly, as in wild type cells, low-level expression of Rtn4a in Lnp knock-out cells resulted in restoration of the tubular network (Figure 10B; fourth column), whereas at higher levels it caused the appearance of long tubules and membrane fragments (not shown).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 10B.

claim: At higher levels of Rtn4a expression in Lnp knock-out cells, it caused the appearance of long tubules and membrane fragments.
source: Similarly, as in wild type cells, low-level expression of Rtn4a in Lnp knock-out cells resulted in restoration of the tubular network (Figure 10B; fourth column), whereas at higher levels it caused the appearance of long tubules and membrane fragments (not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments.

claim: At elevated levels, ATL and Rtn do not depend on Lnp function.
source: These results show that, at elevated levels, ATL and Rtn do not depend on Lnp function.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that ATL and Rtn can restore network morphology in Lnp knockout cells.

claim: When purified cytLnp was added to a crude extract at the beginning of a network formation reaction, small sheets appeared over time, which replaced three-way tubular junctions.
source: Indeed, when purified cytLnp was added to a crude extract at the beginning of a network formation reaction, small sheets appeared over time, which replaced three-way tubular junctions (Figure 11B; the reduction of three-way junctions is quantitated in Figure 11C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 11B and quantified in Figure 11C.

claim: The tubules of the network became shorter when cytLnp was added.
source: In addition, the tubules of the network became shorter.
evidence: This is observed in the microscopy images.

claim: The number of three-way junctions was also reduced when cytLnp was added to a network formation reaction performed with membranes and cytosol.
source: The number of three-way junctions was also reduced when cytLnp was added to a network formation reaction performed with membranes and cytosol (Figure 11D) or with membranes alone (Figure 11—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 11D and Figure 11—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Three-way junctions were also abolished when cytLnp was added after network formation.
source: Three-way junctions were also abolished when cytLnp was added after network formation (Figure 11—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 11—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Affinity-purified antibodies raised against Xenopus Lnp had the same effect as cytLnp on three-way junctions.
source: Affinity-purified antibodies raised against Xenopus Lnp had the same effect (Figure 11E and Figure 11—figure supplement 1C), confirming that Lnp inactivation causes the change in ER morphology.
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 11E and Figure 11—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A C-terminal fragment of cytLnp (cytLnp-C) had the same effect on the integrity of three-way junctions as cytLnp.
source: A C-terminal fragment of cytLnp (cytLnp-C) had the same effect on the integrity of three-way junctions as cytLnp, whereas two different N-terminal fragments (cytLnp-N1 and –N2) were inactive (Figure 11F).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 11F.

claim: Two different N-terminal fragments of cytLnp (cytLnp-N1 and –N2) were inactive.
source: A C-terminal fragment of cytLnp (cytLnp-C) had the same effect on the integrity of three-way junctions as cytLnp, whereas two different N-terminal fragments (cytLnp-N1 and –N2) were inactive (Figure 11F).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 11F.

claim: Pull-down experiments confirmed that cytLnp and cytLnp-C, but not cytLnp-N1 or –N2, interact with endogenous Lnp.
source: Pull-down experiments confirmed that cytLnp and cytLnp-C, but not cytLnp-N1 or –N2, interact with endogenous Lnp (Figure 11—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is directly observed in the pull-down experiments shown in Figure 11—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: The Zn2+-finger-containing constructs cytLnp and cytLnp-C likely form inactive oligomers with the endogenous full-length protein.
source: The Zn2+-finger-containing constructs cytLnp and cytLnp-C likely form inactive oligomers with the endogenous full-length protein.
evidence: This is inferred from the interaction data and the dominant-negative effect.

claim: Gel filtration experiments indicated that cytLnp and cytLnp-C form oligomers, in contrast to cytLnp-N1 and cytLnp-N2, which elute as monomers.
source: Consistent with this assumption, gel filtration experiments indicated that cytLnp and cytLnp-C form oligomers, in contrast to cytLnp-N1 and cytLnp-N2, which elute as monomers (Figure 11—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is directly observed in the gel filtration experiments shown in Figure 11—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Lnp stabilizes three-way tubular junctions and tubules.
source: Taken together, these results are consistent with those obtained in mammalian cells, and show that Lnp stabilizes three-way tubular junctions and tubules.
evidence: This is concluded from the experiments with cytLnp and Lnp antibodies.

claim: Lnp-Lnp interactions involving the Zn2+-finger containing domain seem to be required for the function of Lnp.
source: Lnp-Lnp interactions involving the Zn2+-finger containing domain seem to be required for the function of Lnp.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutant analysis and interaction studies.

claim: The network formed with crude Xenopus extracts after addition of cytLnp looks indistinguishable from that in mitosis.
source: The network formed with crude Xenopus extracts after addition of cytLnp looks indistinguishable from that in mitosis, consisting of small sheets connected by multiple, short tubules (compare Figures 11B and 2G).
evidence: This is a comparative observation from the microscopy images.

claim: In both cytLnp-treated and mitotic extracts, the number of three-way junctions was reduced to about the same extent compared with an interphase extract.
source: In both cases, the number of three-way junctions was reduced to about the same extent compared with an interphase extract (Figure 11C).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 11C.

claim: A mitotic network was indistinguishable from an interphase network formed in the presence of cytLnp in a fractionated system consisting of membranes and cytosol.
source: Similar results were obtained with a fractionated system consisting of membranes and cytosol; here too, a mitotic network (Wang et al., 2013) was indistinguishable from an interphase network formed in the presence of cytLnp (Figure 11D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 11D.

claim: The similarity between cytLnp-treated and mitotic networks suggests that Lnp is inactivated during mitosis.
source: The similarity suggests that Lnp is inactivated during mitosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity in ER morphology.

claim: Lnp is phosphorylated in mitotic (meiotic) Xenopus extracts.
source: Lnp is indeed phosphorylated in mitotic (meiotic) Xenopus extracts. Endogenous Lnp, which ran as a single band in interphase extracts, was converted into two higher molecular weight species (Figure 12A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the immunoblots shown in Figure 12A.

claim: Endogenous Lnp, which ran as a single band in interphase extracts, was converted into two higher molecular weight species in mitotic extracts.
source: Lnp is indeed phosphorylated in mitotic (meiotic) Xenopus extracts. Endogenous Lnp, which ran as a single band in interphase extracts, was converted into two higher molecular weight species (Figure 12A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the immunoblots shown in Figure 12A.

claim: The same size shifts were seen with His-tagged cytLnp added to either interphase or mitotic extracts.
source: The same size shifts were seen with His-tagged cytLnp added to either interphase or mitotic extracts (Figure 12B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the immunoblots shown in Figure 12B.

claim: Both higher molecular weight species of Lnp disappeared when cytLnp was pulled down with cobalt beads, indicating that Lnp modification is reversible.
source: Both higher molecular weight species disappeared when cytLnp was pulled down with cobalt beads, indicating that Lnp modification is reversible.
evidence: This is observed in the pull-down experiments.

claim: Addition of phosphatase inhibitors during pull-down resulted in the disappearance of the higher molecular weight species, but preserved the lower one.
source: Addition of phosphatase inhibitors during pull-down resulted in the disappearance of the higher molecular weight species, but preserved the lower one (Figure 12C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the immunoblots shown in Figure 12C.

claim: Addition of N-ethylmaleimide preserved both bands of modified Lnp.
source: Addition of N-ethylmaleimide preserved both bands.
evidence: This is observed in the pull-down experiments.

claim: At least the smaller of the two modified species corresponds to mitotically phosphorylated Lnp.
source: These results indicate that at least the smaller of the two modified species corresponds to mitotically phosphorylated Lnp.
evidence: This is inferred from the effects of phosphatase inhibitors.

claim: It is possible that the larger species carries an additional modification.
source: It is possible that the larger species carries an additional modification.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of two modified species.

claim: Mass spectrometry revealed that Xenopus Lnp is mitotically phosphorylated at multiple sites, most of which are located in the unstructured domain, located between CC2 and the Zn2+-finger domain.
source: Mass spectrometry revealed that Xenopus Lnp is mitotically phosphorylated at multiple sites, most of which are located in the unstructured domain, located between CC2 and the Zn2+-finger domain (Figure 12D).
evidence: This is directly determined by mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 12D.

claim: It is unclear whether all sites are equally modified in a given Lnp molecule.
source: It is unclear whether all sites are equally modified in a given Lnp molecule.
evidence: This is a statement of uncertainty about the phosphorylation pattern.

claim: Lnp is also mitotically phosphorylated in mammalian U2OS cells.
source: Lnp is also mitotically phosphorylated in mammalian U2OS cells. Immunoblotting showed that endogenous Lnp increases in size and decreases in abundance in cells arrested in mitosis with the microtubule-depolymerizing drug nocodazole (Figure 12E).
evidence: This is directly observed in the immunoblots shown in Figure 12E.

claim: Endogenous Lnp increases in size and decreases in abundance in cells arrested in mitosis with the microtubule-depolymerizing drug nocodazole.
source: Immunoblotting showed that endogenous Lnp increases in size and decreases in abundance in cells arrested in mitosis with the microtubule-depolymerizing drug nocodazole (Figure 12E).
evidence: This is directly observed in the immunoblots shown in Figure 12E.

claim: Like other proteins regulated during the cell cycle in mammalian cells, Lnp seems to be degraded following phosphorylation.
source: Like other proteins regulated during the cell cycle in mammalian cells, Lnp seems to be degraded following phosphorylation.
evidence: This is inferred from the decrease in abundance during mitosis.

claim: Overexpressed Lnp-mCherry underwent a size shift during mitosis and slightly increased in abundance when its degradation was prevented by addition of the proteasome inhibitor bortezomib.
source: Overexpressed Lnp-mCherry also underwent a size shift during mitosis and slightly increased in abundance when its degradation was prevented by addition of the proteasome inhibitor bortezomib (Figure 12F).
evidence: This is directly observed in the immunoblots shown in Figure 12F.

claim: A Lnp-mCherry mutant in which phosphorylation sites were mutated to Ala did not undergo a size shift in mitosis nor a change in abundance with bortezomib treatment.
source: A Lnp-mCherry mutant in which phosphorylation sites were mutated to Ala did not undergo a size shift in mitosis nor a change in abundance with bortezomib treatment.
evidence: This is observed in the immunoblots.

claim: The mitotic phosphorylation sites in mammalian Lnp were in the same domain as in Xenopus Lnp.
source: The mitotic phosphorylation sites in mammalian Lnp were in the same domain as in Xenopus Lnp (Figure 12D).
evidence: This is shown in the alignment in Figure 12D.

claim: Pull-down experiments showed that the oligomerization of cytLnp is weakened in mitotic Xenopus extracts.
source: Pull-down experiments showed that the oligomerization of cytLnp is weakened in mitotic Xenopus extracts (Figure 12—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the pull-down experiments shown in Figure 12—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A phosphomimetic cytLnp mutant containing several Ser/Thr to Glu mutations (cytLnp-E) had a weakened tendency to oligomerize.
source: A phosphomimetic cytLnp mutant containing several Ser/Thr to Glu mutations (cytLnp-E) also had a weakened tendency to oligomerize (Figure 12—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the pull-down experiments shown in Figure 12—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Mitotic phosphorylation reduces the interaction of Lnp molecules, which in turn leads to the destabilization of three-way junctions and tubules.
source: These results suggest that mitotic phosphorylation reduces the interaction of Lnp molecules, which in turn leads to the destabilization of three-way junctions and tubules.
evidence: This is inferred from the oligomerization and localization studies.

claim: A phosphomimetic mutant of full-length Lnp did not localize to three-way junctions when expressed at low levels in CRISPR knock-out cells.
source: Consistent with this model, a phosphomimetic mutant of full-length Lnp did not localize to three-way junctions when expressed at low levels in CRISPR knock-out cells, in contrast to a mutant in which the same residues were changed to Ala (Figure 12—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 12—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: A mutant of full-length Lnp in which phosphorylation sites were changed to Ala localized to three-way junctions when expressed at low levels in CRISPR knock-out cells.
source: Consistent with this model, a phosphomimetic mutant of full-length Lnp did not localize to three-way junctions when expressed at low levels in CRISPR knock-out cells, in contrast to a mutant in which the same residues were changed to Ala (Figure 12—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the microscopy images shown in Figure 12—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Mitotic phosphorylation may cause the disappearance of Lnp from three-way junctions; the junctions are then converted into larger sheets.
source: Thus, mitotic phosphorylation may cause the disappearance of Lnp from three-way junctions; the junctions are then converted into larger sheets.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental observations.
